title: Never Work: from the Rue du Four to the House at Champot
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Paris, 20th arrondissement: birth of Guy-Ernest Debord
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day (FR and EN Wikipedia). Coordinates are the civic center of the arrondissement, Place Gambetta; no street address is given in any source consulted.
stops.campa: Guy-Ernest Debord is born in the twentieth arrondissement of Paris, in the quarter where his mother's father keeps a small business in luxury shoes. His father Martial is a pharmacist; his mother is Paulette Rossi. The pharmacist dies young, and the widow sends the boy for long stretches to his grandmother in Italy, the first of the displacements that will carry him down the length of France before he is fifteen. Of the apartment itself, the street, the rooms, the registers consulted here keep nothing.
suggested_refs: The civil registers of the 20th arrondissement, 28 December 1931

stops.name: Nice: the family leaves Paris for the coast
stops.date_confidence: attested to the autumn of 1939 (FR Wikipedia); month set to September as the start of that season. Coordinates corrected to Place Massena, 43.6973 / 7.2701; an earlier figure of 7.2761 fell some 480 m east, in the Paillon gardens.
stops.campa: War comes, and the household leaves Paris for the coast. Debord is seven. Nice in the autumn of 1939 is still a city of promenades and hotels filling with people who have decided the fighting will happen somewhere else. The boy has already lost his father and has already been sent away once, to a grandmother in Italy. He will spend the whole war being moved: one town, one lycee, one set of classmates at a time, none of them long enough to belong to. The address the family takes in Nice is not recorded.
suggested_refs: Place Massena, taken as the central reference point for the family's arrival in Nice

stops.name: Fontainebleau, College Carnot: a year in the occupied zone
stops.date_confidence: attested to the summer of 1941 (FR Wikipedia); month set to July within that summer. An earlier draft flagged a 1941/1942 contradiction between the English and French summaries; on re-reading, both give Fontainebleau 1941 and Pau 1942, and the contradiction does not exist.
stops.campa: The family moves inland to Fontainebleau, and Debord is enrolled at the College Carnot. He is nine, in the middle of an occupied country, in a forest town whose chateau the Germans use and whose school runs on the rationed normality of the period. Fontainebleau is a garrison town for the occupier and a school town for everyone else, and the two arrangements share the same streets. The stay lasts a year. The French and English accounts of these wartime moves agree on the sequence: Fontainebleau in the summer of 1941, Pau in the summer of 1942.
suggested_refs: The College Carnot at Fontainebleau, enrolment of 1941

stops.name: Pau, Lycee Louis-Barthou: two years at the foot of the Pyrenees
stops.date_confidence: attested to the summer of 1942 in both the English and French summaries; month set to July within that summer.
stops.campa: The household settles at Pau, under the Pyrenees, and the boy enters the Lycee Louis-Barthou. Pau is deep in the unoccupied zone in the summer of 1942, and by November it is not: the Germans come south across the demarcation line and the distinction ends. Debord is ten, then eleven, here. On clear days the Pyrenees stand along the whole southern edge of the town, and the Spanish border behind them. What he read, or was taught, or refused to be taught in these two years survives in no source consulted; the name of the lycee is nearly all the record gives.
suggested_refs: The Lycee Louis-Barthou at Pau, attended 1942-1945

stops.name: Cannes, Lycee Carnot: six years and the cinema
stops.date_confidence: attested to March 1945 for the family's arrival, and to June 1951 for the baccalaureat, in both the English and French summaries.
stops.campa: In March 1945 the family establishes itself at Cannes, and Debord enters the Lycee Carnot, where he stays six years, through the baccalaureat of June 1951. Cannes is where the cinema takes hold of him. The town rebuilds itself around a film festival while he is a schoolboy in it, and he learns to watch films as someone who intends both to make one and to wreck one. The hall of the first festivals stands a few streets from the lycee, and the town fills every spring with people whose profession is the projection of images. He is fourteen when he arrives and nineteen when he leaves.
suggested_refs: The Lycee Carnot at Cannes, March 1945 to June 1951

stops.name: Cannes, the film festival: meeting Isidore Isou
stops.date_confidence: attested to the April 1951 Cannes festival (FR Wikipedia). Britannica's 'about age eighteen' and its 1950 dating are not followed: they conflict with the documented baccalaureat of June 1951 and the move to Paris that followed it.
stops.campa: At the film festival of April 1951 Debord meets Isidore Isou and the Lettrists, who have come to Cannes to show Isou's Traite de bave et d'eternite and to make as much noise about it as the hall will bear. The Lettrists attack language itself, breaking poetry down to the letter and film down to scratched stock and shouting. Debord finds the thing he will do next. He is nineteen, two months short of the baccalaureat, sitting in a room where a film is being howled down.
suggested_refs: Isidore Isou, 'Traite de bave et d'eternite', shown at Cannes in April 1951
sources: Britannica, 'Guy Debord' (date not followed, see confidence note)

stops.name: Paris, rue du Four: the law faculty abandoned for a bar
stops.date_confidence: the move to Paris and the brief law enrolment are attested to 1951; the October date is the ordinary start of the academic year and is a placeholder within the attested year. The bar is documented as the Lettrist International's headquarters from 1952.
stops.campa: Debord comes up to Paris, enrols in law, and stops going. What he attends instead is a bar: Chez Moineau, on the rue du Four in Saint-Germain-des-Pres, where the youngest and least employable of the Lettrists drink, sleep on other people's floors, and steal. The regulars are teenagers, deserters and the unpublishable. This is the milieu out of which the Lettrist International comes, and it will not survive intact five years. He never takes the degree.
suggested_refs: Chez Moineau, rue du Four, headquarters of the Lettrist International 1952-1957

stops.name: Paris, Musee de l'Homme: the premiere of Hurlements en faveur de Sade
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day: premiere 30 June 1952 at the cine-club d'avant-garde of the Musee de l'Homme, interrupted in the first minutes; first complete screening 13 October 1952 at the Cine-club du Quartier Latin (FR Wikipedia).
stops.campa: The cine-club d'avant-garde at the Musee de l'Homme screens Hurlements en faveur de Sade. There are no images. White screen carries the voices of Gil J Wolman, Debord, Serge Berna, Barbara Rosenthal and Isidore Isou; black screen carries nothing at all, and the film ends in twenty-four minutes of silent black. The organisers cut it off within the first minutes. The complete version is shown that October, at the Cine-club du Quartier Latin, to an audience that has been warned.
suggested_refs: 'Hurlements en faveur de Sade' (1952), soundtrack and blank screen, first shown at the Palais de Chaillot

stops.name: Paris: the Lettrist International breaks from Isou
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1952 (Britannica; EN Wikipedia); the month is not established in the sources consulted and December is a placeholder within the attested year.
stops.campa: The Lettrists split. Debord, pushed by Gil J Wolman, leads a breakaway that takes the name Lettrist International and treats Isou as an obstacle rather than a master. The quarrel is over tactics, and over who is permitted to be serious. Its programme is the abolition of work and the construction of situations, and it holds that a career is a form of surrender. The new group has no money and no publication anyone reads, and its whole membership fits around one table at Chez Moineau.
suggested_refs: The founding documents of the Lettrist International, 1952

stops.name: Paris, rue de Seine: NE TRAVAILLEZ JAMAIS
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1953 (EN Wikipedia); no month or day is recorded, and the date defaults to 1 January of the attested year.
stops.campa: On a wall in the rue de Seine, Debord writes NE TRAVAILLEZ JAMAIS. Never work. He is twenty-one and has no intention of holding a job, and the phrase will outlive every organisation he founds. Chalk on stone, at night, in a street of galleries and bookshops, costing nothing and taking a minute. No month or day is recorded for it. Someone photographs the wall. That photograph circulates for decades, is reprinted on postcards, and is eventually sold.
suggested_refs: The photographed wall of the rue de Seine, 'Ne travaillez jamais'

stops.name: Paris: 'Introduction to a Critique of Urban Geography'
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1955, in the Belgian review Les Levres nues (Wikipedia, 'Derive'); the month is not fixed in the sources consulted and September is a placeholder within the attested year. Coordinates are a Latin Quarter reference point, not a publication address.
stops.campa: In the Belgian review Les Levres nues, Debord publishes 'Introduction a une critique de la geographie urbaine.' The argument: a city acts on the people crossing it, quarter by quarter, in ways planners neither intend nor notice, and that action can be studied. He names the study psychogeography. Ivan Chtcheglov had already written the poem of the idea two years earlier, at nineteen, in a formulary aimed straight at Le Corbusier and at the Plan Voisin that proposed to flatten central Paris into towers in a park. Debord gives it a method.
suggested_refs: Les Levres nues no. 6 (1955); Ivan Chtcheglov, 'Formulaire pour un urbanisme nouveau' (1953)

stops.name: Amsterdam: the derives by walkie-talkie
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The account, attributed to Henri Lefebvre, places coordinated derives by walkie-talkie first in Amsterdam and later in Strasbourg, but fixes no date; the secondary literature gives only 'the 1950s'. The year here is a placeholder inside that decade and should not be read as attested.
stops.campa: Accounts of the early derives, one of them attributed to Henri Lefebvre, describe situationists crossing a city in separate parties, in touch by walkie-talkie, first in Amsterdam and later in Strasbourg. Two or three people drift; the others radio in what the streets are doing to them. It is a drift with a control room, an experiment run on the experimenters. Lefebvre, who knew them well and later fell out with them badly, is the source most often cited for the detail.
suggested_refs: Henri Lefebvre's recollections of the early situationist derives
sources: Wikipedia, 'Derive' (attributing the account to Henri Lefebvre; dates uncertain)

stops.name: Paris: 'A User's Guide to Detournement'
stops.date_confidence: attested to May 1956, Les Levres nues no. 8 (Wikipedia, 'Detournement'). Coordinates are a Latin Quarter reference point, not a publication address.
stops.campa: Debord and Gil J Wolman publish 'Mode d'emploi du detournement' in Les Levres nues. The method: take what already exists, a film, a comic strip, a slogan, an advertisement, and turn it against itself by putting it where it was never meant to go. They rank the procedures, and hold simple reversal to be the weakest of them. They open by quoting a maxim on plagiarism that they expect nobody to have understood. The words are Lautreamont's, from the Poesies, and Debord will take them again, unattributed, in thesis 207 of the book he writes eleven years later.
stops.quote: Detournement by simple reversal is always the most direct and the least effective.
stops.quote_source: Guy Debord and Gil J Wolman, 'A User's Guide to Detournement' (Les Levres nues no. 8, May 1956), trans. Ken Knabb
suggested_refs: Lautreamont, 'Poesies' II (1870), the source of the plagiarism maxim the essay quotes

stops.name: Paris: 'Theory of the Derive'
stops.date_confidence: attested to November 1956, Les Levres nues no. 9. Note that this is not the first public statement of the idea: the 1955 'Introduction to a Critique of Urban Geography' preceded it in the same journal. It is the fullest early statement.
stops.campa: 'Theorie de la derive' appears in the ninth number of Les Levres nues. A derive is a technique of rapid passage through varied ambiances: one or more persons drop their work, their leisure and their reasons for going anywhere, and let the terrain pull them. Debord takes the practice off the Surrealists and strips the marvellous out of it, leaving a map and a stopwatch. Thirty years earlier Andre Breton had walked Paris for ten days with Nadja on something close to this principle, reading the signs the city offered him and calling the result chance.
stops.quote: In a derive one or more persons during a certain period drop their relations, their work and leisure activities, and all their other usual motives for movement and action, and let themselves be drawn by the attractions of the terrain and the encounters they find there.
stops.quote_source: Guy Debord, 'Theory of the Derive' (1956; reprinted Internationale Situationniste no. 2, 1958), trans. Ken Knabb
suggested_refs: Andre Breton, 'Nadja' (1928), the acknowledged ancestor of the derive

stops.name: Cosio d'Arroscia: the founding of the Situationist International
stops.date_confidence: attested to 27-28 July 1957 (EN Wikipedia, 'Situationist International'; FR Wikipedia, 'Guy Debord'). Two coordinate sets for the village circulate in the material behind this file, 44.0937 / 7.8207 and 44.0964 / 7.8181, roughly 400 m apart; the first is used here and the discrepancy is left standing, not resolved.
stops.campa: Delegates of three groups meet in a village in the Ligurian hills in the last days of July and merge: the Lettrist International, the International Movement for an Imaginist Bauhaus, and the London Psychogeographical Association. Debord arrives with the report he has written for the occasion, which argues that the world must be changed and that the way to change it is to build situations, concrete constructions of momentary ambiences. Asger Jorn brings the painters. The Situationist International exists from that week, and will last fifteen years.
stops.quote: First of all, we think the world must be changed. We want the most liberating change of the society and life in which we find ourselves confined.
stops.quote_source: Guy Debord, 'Report on the Construction of Situations' (1957), trans. Ken Knabb
suggested_refs: The 'Rapport sur la construction des situations' (1957), founding text read at Cosio d'Arroscia

stops.name: Paris, first conference of the SI: the vocabulary printed
stops.date_confidence: attested to 25-26 January 1958 (FR Wikipedia, 'Internationale situationniste'). The venue is not named in the sources consulted; coordinates mark the Latin Quarter as a general reference.
stops.campa: The first conference of the Situationist International meets in Paris over two days at the end of January. The first number of the journal Internationale Situationniste follows, and it opens with definitions set out like dictionary entries: derive, detournement, psychogeography, situationist. A group six months old issues its own vocabulary before it has an office. Where in Paris the delegates actually sat is not recorded in the accounts consulted.
suggested_refs: Internationale Situationniste no. 1 (June 1958), the definitions page

stops.name: Munich, third conference of the SI
stops.date_confidence: attested to 17-20 April 1959 (FR Wikipedia, 'Internationale situationniste').
stops.campa: The third conference meets at Munich in the middle of April and sits for four days. By now the group has sections in several countries, and they bring with them the argument that will run through every conference it holds: whether situationists are making art or abolishing it. The painters in the room want the first answer. Debord gives the second, and does not change it over the next fifteen years. What else the Munich sessions settled, the published accounts do not say.
suggested_refs: Proceedings of the third SI conference, Munich, April 1959

stops.name: Paris: signing the Manifesto of the 121
stops.date_confidence: attested to September 1960 (EN Wikipedia, 'Guy Debord'); the day of Debord's signature is not recorded in the sources consulted.
stops.campa: Debord signs the Declaration on the Right of Insubordination in the Algerian War, the text known as the Manifesto of the 121. It defends desertion and refusal of service in a war the French state is still calling a police operation. The day he puts his name to it is not recorded. Andre Breton signs the same paper, and so does most of the Surrealist and existentialist Paris that Debord has spent the decade attacking in print. Signatories lose broadcasting work, and some are prosecuted.
suggested_refs: 'Declaration sur le droit a l'insoumission dans la guerre d'Algerie' (September 1960), list of signatories

stops.name: London, fourth conference of the SI
stops.date_confidence: attested to 24-28 September 1960 (EN and FR Wikipedia).
stops.campa: The fourth conference meets in London, and the fracture that will never close opens there. The painters want a movement of new art; the theorists want a movement against art as such. Debord is with the second party, and from London onward disagreements inside the group are settled by exclusion rather than by compromise. Under that quarrel lies a harder one, which the London sessions put and do not answer: what is the revolutionary proletariat now, and does it survive in countries of full employment and television?
suggested_refs: Minutes of the fourth SI conference, London, September 1960

stops.name: Gothenburg, fifth conference of the SI
stops.date_confidence: attested to 28-30 August 1961 (FR Wikipedia, 'Internationale situationniste'). Whether Debord attended in person is not stated in the sources consulted.
stops.campa: The fifth conference meets at Gothenburg over three days at the end of August; whether Debord is in the room is not stated in the sources consulted. The Scandinavian and German sections want the group to stay a laboratory of new art. The French want it to stop producing anything that can be hung, sold or reviewed. He is twenty-nine and has been directing an organisation for four years without ever having held a job. Within a year the exclusions begin and the artists go.
suggested_refs: Proceedings of the fifth SI conference, Gothenburg, August 1961

stops.name: Antwerp, sixth conference of the SI
stops.date_confidence: attested to 12-16 November 1962 (FR Wikipedia, 'Internationale situationniste'). Whether Debord attended in person is not stated in the sources consulted.
stops.campa: The sixth conference meets at Antwerp in November. The break with the artists has happened. What remains is a small body of theorists who publish a journal, sell nothing, and expel one another with a formality outsiders find comic. Debord is thirty-one, and the organisation he leads would fit into one large room. It has begun writing about a revolt of the young that has not happened yet. The journal goes on appearing, numbered, austere, much of it unsigned.
suggested_refs: Proceedings of the sixth SI conference, Antwerp, November 1962

stops.name: Paris, seventh conference of the SI: the Minimum Definition
stops.date_confidence: attested to 5-11 July 1966 (FR Wikipedia, 'Internationale situationniste'). The venue is not named; coordinates mark the Latin Quarter as a general reference.
stops.campa: The seventh conference meets in Paris in July and sits for a week. It adopts the Minimum Definition of Revolutionary Organizations, a text of a few pages binding the group to workers' councils and against every hierarchy, its own included. It is drafted for an organisation of a few dozen people. Debord is thirty-four and has been running that organisation for nine years, since the week at Cosio d'Arroscia. Two years later the text will be circulating in the occupied Sorbonne.
suggested_refs: 'Definition minimum des organisations revolutionnaires' (July 1966)

stops.name: Strasbourg, Palais Universitaire: the student union scandal
stops.date_confidence: attested to November 1966 (EN Wikipedia, 'On the Poverty of Student Life'); no day is given. Coordinates corrected to the Palais universitaire, 48.5848 / 7.7624; an earlier figure of 48.582 / 7.7677 fell some 500 m southeast of the building.
stops.campa: Five students with situationist sympathies get themselves elected to the Strasbourg student union and spend its funds printing ten thousand copies of a pamphlet, De la misere en milieu etudiant, written largely by Mustapha Khayati. It attacks the university, the student, and the whole apparatus of authorised revolt. The scandal runs through the national press and out of the country, and within weeks a group nobody had heard of is being read by students who have never met a situationist. A court orders the union closed.
suggested_refs: Mustapha Khayati, 'De la misere en milieu etudiant' (Strasbourg, November 1966)
sources: Wikipedia (EN), 'On the Poverty of Student Life'

stops.name: Paris: Buchet-Chastel publishes La Societe du Spectacle
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1967, Buchet-Chastel, Paris; November is given in one summary and the month is not corroborated elsewhere in the sources consulted. Coordinates are a Latin Quarter reference point, not the publisher's address.
stops.campa: Buchet-Chastel publishes La Societe du Spectacle: two hundred and twenty-one numbered theses, the first of which detourns the opening sentence of Karl Marx's Capital, replacing an immense accumulation of commodities with an immense accumulation of spectacles. The spectacle, Debord writes, is not a collection of images but a social relation among people, mediated by images. The book carries the old quarrel of the First International inside it, the Marx of the theses and the anti-authoritarian current running down from Mikhail Bakunin. In 1970 an unauthorised English translation by Fredy Perlman appears from Black and Red in Detroit.
stops.quote: The spectacle is not a collection of images, but a social relation among people, mediated by images.
stops.quote_source: Guy Debord, The Society of the Spectacle (1967), thesis 4, trans. Black and Red (1977)
suggested_refs: The first Buchet-Chastel edition (1967); the Black and Red edition (Detroit, 1970, rev. 1977), trans. Fredy Perlman
sources: marxists.org text of the Black and Red translation

stops.name: Nanterre: the Enrages form on the western edge of Paris
stops.date_confidence: attested to early February 1968 (FR Wikipedia, 'Internationale situationniste'); no day is given. Coordinates corrected to the Nanterre campus, 48.9039 / 2.2138; an earlier figure of 48.8918 fell some 1.35 km south, near Nanterre-Prefecture.
stops.campa: At the university of Nanterre, on the western edge of Paris, students who have read the Strasbourg pamphlet form a group calling itself the Enrages, after the extremists of 1793. The campus is new, raised on cleared ground on the edge of the city, and disliked by nearly everyone made to attend it. There are a handful of them. They break up lectures, insult the sociology faculty, and are handled by the administration as a disciplinary matter to be processed in the usual way. In March the campus goes into open revolt. In May the country does.
suggested_refs: The Enrages of Nanterre, February to March 1968

stops.name: Paris, the Sorbonne: the occupation
stops.date_confidence: attested to 14-17 May 1968 for the occupation and the first Occupation Committee. Two coordinate sets for the Sorbonne appear in the material behind this file, 48.848 / 2.3437 and 48.8489 / 2.3436, about 100 m apart; the first is used and the difference is noted rather than resolved.
stops.campa: Students occupy the Sorbonne, and situationists and Enrages take places on the Occupation Committee of the first days. Debord is in the building. On walls across Paris that month appear sentences lifted from the group's journals and from his own books. Two dozen people hear their vocabulary in the mouths of millions, which is not the same thing as having a following. The phrase he chalked on the rue de Seine fifteen years earlier is back, at the scale of a city: ne travaillez jamais.
suggested_refs: Photographs of the May 1968 wall inscriptions and the Occupation Committee tracts

stops.name: Paris, Centre Censier: the Council for Maintaining the Occupations
stops.date_confidence: attested to May 1968, with dissolution on 15 June 1968 (EN Wikipedia, 'Situationist International'); the exact founding day of the CMDO is not given in the sources consulted.
stops.campa: From the Centre Censier the situationists and their allies run the Conseil pour le maintien des occupations, printing tracts that tell strikers to hold the factories and to give power to workers' councils rather than to the unions negotiating on their behalf. The tracts go out to the plants, past the student milieu, in tens of thousands. Then de Gaulle returns, the elections are called, the plants reopen. The CMDO dissolves on the fifteenth of June.
suggested_refs: Tracts of the Conseil pour le maintien des occupations, May-June 1968

stops.name: Venice, eighth and last conference of the SI
stops.date_confidence: attested to 16 September - 1 October 1969 (EN Wikipedia, 'Situationist International'). The twelfth and final number of Internationale Situationniste, carrying the group's analysis of May, belongs to the same autumn.
stops.campa: The eighth and last conference meets in Venice from the middle of September into October, in the same weeks that the twelfth number of Internationale Situationniste carries the group's account of May. The organisation was never larger than a few dozen and is smaller now. The argument at Venice is how the survivors of a success are to survive it, and no answer is agreed. Membership contracts toward Debord and Gianfranco Sanguinetti. Number twelve is the last one printed.
suggested_refs: Internationale Situationniste no. 12 (September 1969), the last number

stops.name: Paris: the Situationist International dissolves itself
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1972 (EN Wikipedia, 'Guy Debord' and 'Situationist International'); the month is not fixed in the sources consulted and the date defaults to 1 January of the attested year.
stops.campa: Debord and Sanguinetti wind up what is left of the Situationist International, and the two of them are what is left. The dissolution is itself an argument: an organisation that outlives its usefulness turns into the thing it opposed, an opposition available for consumption, a spectacle of refusal. La Veritable Scission dans l'Internationale carries the reasoning, and the last of the expulsions with it. Debord is forty. He has spent twenty years inside groups he founded. He will spend the next twenty-two inside none.
suggested_refs: Debord and Sanguinetti, 'La Veritable Scission dans l'Internationale' (1972)

stops.name: Paris: marriage to Alice Becker-Ho
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day, 2 August 1972 (FR Wikipedia, 'Alice Becker-Ho'). They met in 1963 and were living together well before the marriage. The 1954 marriage to Michele Bernstein is reconstruction: no source consulted here gives its date.
stops.campa: Debord marries Alice Becker-Ho on the second of August. They met in 1963 and have lived together for years. She is a linguist who will spend her life on the argot of the Romani and of the dangerous classes, the languages of people who need not to be understood by the authorities. She is his second wife; Michele Bernstein, the first, was his collaborator through the Lettrist and early situationist years and wrote novels that helped pay for the group.
suggested_refs: Alice Becker-Ho, 'Les Princes du jargon' (1990), on the argot of the dangerous classes

stops.name: Champot Bas, le Minour: the house in the Haute-Loire
stops.date_confidence: attested as '1972 onward' for the retreat to Champot; the month is a placeholder inside that year. Coordinates corrected to the commune of Bellevue-la-Montagne, 45.2217 / 3.8208; two earlier figures, 45.1728 / 3.7797 and 45.1975 / 3.7567, disagree with each other and both fall several kilometres southwest of the commune.
stops.campa: The house is called le Minour, at Champot Bas, in the commune of Bellevue-la-Montagne in the Haute-Loire: stone walls, a hearth, a view of nothing in particular, several hours from Paris by any road. No source consulted places it more precisely than the commune. Debord and Becker-Ho keep it for the rest of his life, and for twenty years Paris will not be sure where he is. Here he reads Clausewitz and the memoirists of the seventeenth century, drinks steadily, and receives almost nobody.
suggested_refs: The mas le Minour at Champot Bas, commune of Bellevue-la-Montagne

stops.name: Paris: the film of La Societe du Spectacle
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1973 (EN Wikipedia, 'The Society of the Spectacle'); no month given. The reported continuous run of the film at a cinema in the rue Cujas, funded by Lebovici, is a reconstruction: it was not confirmed against any source in this pass.
stops.campa: Debord makes a film of La Societe du Spectacle, and it does not illustrate the book. The theses are read aloud over stolen footage: newsreels, Soviet parades, Hollywood cavalry charges, advertisements, riot police, soft pornography, all of it detourned, none of it shot by him. The spectacle is made to comment on itself in its own images. Gerard Lebovici, whose Editions Champ Libre was founded in October 1969, pays for the film, and later keeps it running for years in a Latin Quarter cinema.
suggested_refs: 'La Societe du spectacle' (1973), 88 minutes, entirely of detourned footage

stops.name: Florence and Tuscany: the Italian sojourns
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The French summary gives only 'from the 1970s onward' for the regular Italian stays; 1975 is a placeholder inside that decade, and no arrival or departure date is attested.
stops.campa: From the middle of the decade Debord spends long stretches in Italy, in Florence and the Tuscan countryside, moving between there, Champot and Paris on no announced schedule. No Tuscan address appears in any source consulted. Italy in these years is in its own long crisis of bombs and strategy, and Gianfranco Sanguinetti, the last other situationist, publishes a hoax pamphlet in the voice of a lucid reactionary which the Italian press takes for the real thing and answers seriously.
suggested_refs: Gianfranco Sanguinetti's 1975 pamphlet published under the name Censor

stops.name: Paris: In girum imus nocte et consumimur igni
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1978 (EN Wikipedia, 'Guy Debord'); no month is given in the sources consulted.
stops.campa: Debord makes In girum imus nocte et consumimur igni, a Latin palindrome: we go round in the night and are consumed by fire. The film is an autobiography that declines to explain itself. It is addressed to a generation that lost, and it spends its length on a Paris that no longer exists, on the friends of Chez Moineau, dead or scattered or respectable, and on the flat assertion that he regrets nothing he did with them. It runs in Paris and hardly anywhere else. He is forty-six.
suggested_refs: 'In girum imus nocte et consumimur igni' (1978), the last of the six films

stops.name: Seville: an apartment in Spain
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The French summary gives only 'the 1980s' for the Seville apartment; 1980 is a placeholder inside that decade. Coordinates mark the Santa Cruz quarter as a general reference; no address is established.
stops.campa: Debord rents an apartment in Seville and spends part of the decade in Spain. He is fifty, translated into a dozen languages, quoted by people who have not read him, and reachable by almost nobody. Spain is four years out of a dictatorship and the Andalusian summer is unbearable by ten in the morning. The films are the only thing of his anyone can see, and outside Paris even those are hard to find. Of the Seville years the record keeps the fact of an apartment and little more: not the street, not the neighbours, not what he was writing.
suggested_refs: The Santa Cruz quarter of Seville, general reference for the 1980s apartment

stops.name: Paris, 41 avenue Foch: Lebovici is shot in the parking garage
stops.date_confidence: attested to 5 March 1984, with the body discovered on 7 March (FR Wikipedia, 'Gerard Lebovici'). Two coordinate sets for the garage appear in the material behind this file, 48.8725 / 2.284 and 48.8712 / 2.2823, about 200 m apart; the first is used and the difference is left standing.
stops.campa: Gerard Lebovici parks in the underground garage at 41 avenue Foch and is shot four times in the back of the neck. Three .22 Long Rifle casings lie on the floor of the car; a fourth stands upright on the ledge of the rear window. His identity papers are gone. The body is found two days later. Lebovici had produced Debord's films, published his books, and made himself the one man in Paris with money whom Debord did not treat as an enemy. Nobody is ever charged.
suggested_refs: The unsolved case file of the Lebovici murder, 5 March 1984

stops.name: France: the films withdrawn from circulation
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The withdrawal is widely reported in secondary accounts of Debord's later life and dated only to 1984; no primary source was checked in this pass, and the month here is a placeholder set after the March murder rather than an attested date.
stops.campa: The press turns the murder into a serial about Debord: the sinister theorist, the rich patron, the sect. He answers by pulling his films out of circulation altogether, so that for the rest of his life there is nothing of his to watch and only pages to read. A body of work that had argued about images for twenty years takes its own images off the market. To the lawyer Thierry Levy he writes, days after the killing, denying that he held any power over Lebovici at all.
stops.quote: I deny having any 'power' of any kind, other than that power that Gerard and several others have recognized in me with respect to my merits in social theory and the art of this century.
stops.quote_source: Guy Debord, letter to Thierry Levy, 23 March 1984, trans. NOT BORED! (2007)
suggested_refs: Debord's correspondence of March 1984, translated at notbored.org
sources: Secondary accounts of Debord's later life (withdrawal of the films)

stops.name: Paris: Considerations sur l'assassinat de Gerard Lebovici
stops.date_confidence: attested to February 1985 (FR Wikipedia, 'Gerard Lebovici'). Coordinates are a Latin Quarter reference point; no publication address is established in the sources consulted.
stops.campa: Debord publishes Considerations sur l'assassinat de Gerard Lebovici. The book does not defend him against the newspapers; it prosecutes the newspapers, naming the trade of scandal itself and the men who practise it, and points instead toward the anti-terrorist unit run under Paul Barril during the Mitterrand presidency. No investigation follows in that direction, or in any other. To Floriana Lebovici, the widow, now his publisher, he writes about the paper that had led the campaign.
stops.quote: Le Monde must disappear and for us it already has.
stops.quote_source: Guy Debord, letter to Floriana Lebovici, 12 February 1985, trans. NOT BORED!
suggested_refs: 'Considerations sur l'assassinat de Gerard Lebovici' (Editions Gerard Lebovici, 1985)

stops.name: Champot: Commentaires sur la societe du spectacle
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1988; no month is given in the sources consulted, and the date defaults to 1 January of the attested year. Place of writing is taken as Champot, where he was living; the book was published in Paris.
stops.campa: Twenty-one years after the book, Debord publishes Commentaires sur la societe du spectacle. The concentrated spectacle of the dictatorships and the diffuse spectacle of the supermarkets have fused, he argues, into an integrated spectacle that operates everywhere and answers to nobody, with secrecy as its ordinary method and the ruin of the historical record as its by-product. He is fifty-six and writes it at Champot, several hundred kilometres from anyone who will review it. He opens by naming the readership he expects.
stops.quote: These comments are sure to be welcomed by fifty or sixty people.
stops.quote_source: Guy Debord, Comments on the Society of the Spectacle (1988), opening line, English translation PDF, libcom.org
suggested_refs: 'Commentaires sur la societe du spectacle' (Editions Gerard Lebovici, 1988)
sources: libcom.org PDF of the English translation

stops.name: Champot: Panegyrique, volume one
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1989; no month given in the sources consulted, and the date defaults to 1 January of the attested year.
stops.campa: Panegyrique is an autobiography by a man who intends to be his own last witness: no confessions, no explanations, a prose modelled on the seventeenth century, and a long unembarrassed account of drinking. He has drunk, he writes, more than most people who drink. Biographers will use the book, as he knew they would, and every fact in it was put there by him. The polyneuritis that will define his last years has already begun, and it comes from exactly what the book describes.
suggested_refs: 'Panegyrique', tome premier (Editions Gerard Lebovici, 1989)

stops.name: France: Guy Debord, son art et son temps
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1994 for the making of the television film, with Brigitte Cornand; the broadcast month is not established in the sources consulted, and the date defaults to 1 January of the attested year.
stops.campa: With Brigitte Cornand, Debord makes a television film called Guy Debord, son art et son temps. He has agreed at last to be broadcast, and what he hands French television is a programme largely about French television: massacres, ruined cities, adulterated food, dead rivers, presenters. Of his own art there is very little in it. He is sixty-two and has not made a film in sixteen years. Whether he already knew this would be the last thing he made, the record does not say.
suggested_refs: 'Guy Debord, son art et son temps' (1994), made with Brigitte Cornand

stops.name: Champot Bas: the death
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day and to the manner: suicide by gunshot through the heart, late afternoon, 30 November 1994, at the mas le Minour (FR Wikipedia, 'Guy Debord' and 'Bellevue-la-Montagne'). Coordinates standardised to the commune, 45.2217 / 3.8208, against two conflicting earlier figures.
stops.campa: In the late afternoon of the thirtieth of November, at le Minour, in the house he has kept for twenty-two years, Debord shoots himself through the heart. He is sixty-two. The polyneuritis has made the last years painful, and the drinking has not stopped. He leaves no note that settles anything. Whether the act was a decision of the kind his books argue for, or the end of an illness, is a question his readers have divided over ever since, and no source consulted resolves it.
suggested_refs: The mas le Minour at Champot Bas, 30 November 1994

stops.name: Paris, Square du Vert-Galant: the ashes in the Seine
stops.date_confidence: attested to December 1994 (FR Wikipedia, 'Guy Debord'); no day is given in the sources consulted.
stops.campa: His ashes are scattered into the Seine from the point of the Square du Vert-Galant, at the western tip of the Ile de la Cite, where the river divides and closes again. There is no ceremony and no announcement, and the newspapers report the death afterwards. No grave, no stone, no address. The square is a small wedge of trees below the level of the quays, at the oldest point of the city he had spent a lifetime learning to cross badly on purpose. The water carries him west, past quays he had walked at twenty with nowhere to sleep.
suggested_refs: The Square du Vert-Galant, western point of the Ile de la Cite

stops.name: Paris, Bibliotheque nationale de France: the archive made a national treasure
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day, 29 January 2009 (Wikipedia, 'Guy Debord', quoting Christine Albanel). Coordinates are the Bibliotheque nationale de France, which acquired the papers after the classification blocked their sale to Yale.
stops.campa: Fifteen years after his death the Minister of Culture, Christine Albanel, declares Debord's personal archive a tresor national, calls him one of the most important contemporary thinkers, and blocks its sale to the Beinecke Library at Yale. The declaration is dated the twenty-ninth of January. The papers stay in France and enter the Bibliotheque nationale. The manuscripts of a lifelong argument against recuperation become state property, catalogued, conserved, and consulted by appointment.
suggested_refs: The Debord fonds at the Bibliotheque nationale de France, classified 29 January 2009
